summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of mitochondrial myopathy, coronary artery disease, and hypogammaglobulinemia was admitted for a scheduled IVIG infusion, now adjusted to a half-dose every two weeks. Upon admission, he reported baseline symptoms of chest tightness, diaphoresis, nausea, and lightheadedness, which he associates with dehydration due to autonomic dysfunction. He received a 1900cc saline infusion overnight to optimize fluid status. The next day, he was pre-medicated and received 15g of IVIG, after which he developed transient chest tightness, shortness of breath, nausea, and headache—consistent with prior infusion reactions. Serial troponins and EKGs showed no evidence of cardiac ischemia. Symptoms resolved by the following morning. A chronic skin lesion on the left lower extremity, growing over the past month and reminiscent of prior squamous cell carcinoma, was noted, and dermatology follow-up was recommended. The patient remained stable, and no medication changes were made. He was discharged home in good condition with plans to continue outpatient IVIG and follow-up with specialists.
problems: Symptomatic inflammatory myopathy in diseases classified elsewhere
